What exactly happens in a human cell when it's exposed to very high or very low temperatures?
On a cellular level, why are extreme temperatures dangerous?

Well, in extremely high temperatures, the water inside your cells turns to steam, which has a whole shit-ton more volume, and thus this bursts the cells and kills the human.

In cold temperatures, small ice-crystals form, and those things are sharp.
Before the water turns into steam, proteins start to denature (lose the structure that gives them their unique functions) and many chemical reactions within the body speed up or stop happening.
Both gasses and ice expand hence cell rupture in both cases.

Your cells are mostly made from proteins (however the same logic applies elsewhere), and proteins are long chains of molecules. The best way to imagine proteins for our case is to think of them as long strings of magnetic beads. Each bead is magnetic to a different degree which causes the string to fold into strange clumpy shapes. Those shapes are intentional, and it is their shape which causes them to function the way they do.

Heat, at this scale, is most easily represented by everything flipping out and flying around like crazy smacking into everything else at insanely high speeds.

The problem with extreme heats, is that the impact force of the collisions of the particles becomes stronger than the weak magnetism that holds them in their shapes, so they unfold into threads, get tangled with other proteins, punch holes in the sides of stuff, and so on. Essentially your cell as a whole goes from a mixture of parts with unique purposes, to a mush of tangled homogeneous garbage, and the process that you would call "life" stops happening.

By April 2010 Sony was removing OtherOS in response to this. The failoverflow overflow group demonstrated a method of crypographically signing their homebrew meaning the hypervisor would allow it to run. They never published their work and it was geohot that obtained and published failoverflows work which lead to homebrew custom firmware, hypervisor exploits, piracy, and eventually restoration of OtherOS which is still shit because its now extremely dated hardware.
